  • tofu/harbor/main.tf
  • platform/apps/templates/kyverno.yaml
  • platform/apps/templates/trust-manager.yaml
  • spike

docs.title: 0002 — Write every admission policy in Kyverno CEL
docs.text:
In one sentence: Kyverno's legacy policies (ClusterPolicy) are removed in 1.20, so every policy is written in the new CEL types, aligned with native Kubernetes admission.

Status Date Scope Accepted September 2026 Every policy under policies/

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Admission must enforce the image chain of trust (signature and attestations from the build workflow, a catalog base read from the provenance, labels, Harbor as the only registry) and Pod Security restricted in workload namespaces. It must report deviations in platform namespaces, and be testable offline in CI.

Kyverno 1.19 offers two families: the legacy ClusterPolicy/Policy (deprecated, removed in 1.20) and the CEL types (ValidatingPolicy, ImageValidatingPolicy, MutatingPolicy), aligned with Kubernetes' ValidatingAdmissionPolicy. The other candidate was OPA Gatekeeper with Rego.

CEL in a nutshell

Common Expression Language: the small expression language Kubernetes natively uses for its admission rules. A CEL policy reads like a boolean condition on the submitted object.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Every policy uses a CEL type. No ClusterPolicy or Policy in the repository.
    • Workload (enforced): workload-image-signature, workload-golden-base, workload-registry, workload-image-labels.
    • Workload (warning): workload-golden-base-deprecated.
    • Workload (mutation): workload-pod-security, which labels workload namespaces Pod Security restricted.
    • Trust tiers: tier-label (only admins set the tier) and tier-required (any pod outside a valid tier is denied).
    • Platform (audit): platform-registry-allow-list, platform-vendor-signatures.
  • Pod Security restricted is the native Pod Security Admission, not re-implemented as a policy.
  • Policies read their parameters from generated ConfigMaps (golden catalog, allowed registries): a catalog change needs no policy change.
  • Admitted images are rewritten to their digest (mutateDigest).
  • Enforcing policies run with failurePolicy: Fail: if Kyverno does not answer, the pod is denied.
  • Tests: kyverno test (one suite per policy) and Chainsaw on an ephemeral kind cluster, on every pull request.

docs.title: Alternatives set aside
docs.text:
• Legacy ClusterPolicy: removed in Kyverno 1.20, it would be debt from day one.
  • OPA Gatekeeper + Rego: very common in banks, but signature verification needs an external data provider (Ratify) and Rego is one more language to master. A side-by-side comparison stays on the roadmap.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
• CEL policies report fail, never warn: the "deprecated base" case shows as fail in PolicyReports while admission only shows a warning.
  • A denial by a CEL policy emits no Kubernetes event: violations are counted from the API server audit log.
  • kyverno test deadlocks when two image-verifying policies evaluate the same resource (upstream bug kyverno/sdk#125), hence one test suite per policy.

docs.title: What would make me change my mind
docs.text: A client already running Gatekeeper everywhere: I would run the planned comparison before imposing a second engine.

docs.title: 0003 — Kubescape over Trivy Operator and Falco in the cluster
docs.text:
In one sentence: a single operator (Kubescape) covers running-image scanning, posture checks and runtime detection, where the usual combination needs two, which fits a 12 GiB budget.

Status Date Scope Accepted September 2026 In-cluster vulnerability scanning, posture, runtime detection, runtime VEX

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Inside the cluster, we need to:

  • scan the images that are running;
  • check the configuration (CIS controls);
  • detect abnormal behaviour at runtime (a shell opened in a container must raise an alert);
  • ideally, prove that a vulnerable package is never loaded.

The classic pair is Trivy Operator (scanning, posture) plus Falco (runtime rules): two operators, two agents, two rule languages, on a single node capped at 12 GiB.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The Kubescape operator replaces both:

  • scanning of running images with Grype;
  • CIS and NSA controls;
  • runtime detection by the eBPF node-agent, which compares each container's behaviour with a profile (learned, or hand-written as for runtime-demo); alerts are JSON log lines collected by VictoriaLogs;
  • runtime OpenVEX documents (experimental) listing packages never loaded, forwarded by dt-bridge to Dependency-Track.

docs.title: Alternatives set aside
docs.text:
• Trivy Operator + Falco: two complete stacks for the same coverage, too heavy for the memory budget.
  • Falco alone: excellent at runtime, but covers neither scanning nor posture.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
• The cluster scanner (Grype) is not the CI and Harbor scanner (Trivy): their CVE lists diverge. Dependency-Track decides (ADR 0008).
  • Runtime VEX generation is experimental: about two minutes of observation per container, and inconsistent image names (docker.io versus index.docker.io) that dt-bridge normalises.
  • A runtime rule stays silent until the container's profile is loaded. A learned profile only exists after the learning period; a hand-written one exists at once. Hence the hand-written profile for the demo.
  • Falco's large community rule set is lost. Kubescape's default rules cover the demo cases.

docs.title: What would make me change my mind
docs.text: A need for many fine-grained runtime rules (PCI compliance, for instance): Falco would become relevant again, even at the memory cost.

docs.title: 0004 — Triage vulnerabilities in Dependency-Track, fed by an in-house bridge
docs.text:
In one sentence: Dependency-Track is the source of truth for CVE triage, fed with the SBOM signed at build time by dt-bridge, a small Python service filling what Dependency-Track cannot do on its own.

Status Date Scope Accepted September 2026 SBOM storage, vulnerability triage, VEX handling

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every image carries a CycloneDX SBOM attested at build time, and its golden base comes with vendor OpenVEX statements (Docker Hardened Images publishes not_affected statements). Kubescape produces runtime VEX.

Triage needs one place to see flaws per image version and apply VEX, fed with the attested SBOM, not a regenerated one. But Dependency-Track 5.1 imports CycloneDX SBOMs and VEX, not OpenVEX (DependencyTrack/dependency-track#7094), and has no Harbor integration.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Dependency-Track 5.1, on CloudNativePG, is the triage source of truth.
  • dt-bridge, a FastAPI service itself built through the golden path, connects the two:
    • on every Harbor webhook, it reads the image's CycloneDX attestation, verifies its signature against the build identity, and uploads the SBOM unchanged to project <harbor project>/<repository>, version = tag. If the provenance fails verification, nothing is uploaded;
    • it reads the DHI base from the verified provenance, fetches its OpenVEX, converts the not_affected statements into CycloneDX VEX and uploads it once Dependency-Track has analysed the SBOM;
    • it forwards Kubescape's runtime VEX the same way;
    • it exports the posture metrics of the Grafana dashboard.
  • All the OpenVEX vocabulary is isolated in one module (vex.py), removable in one piece the day Dependency-Track imports OpenVEX.

docs.title: Alternatives set aside
docs.text:
• Letting Harbor triage alone: Harbor scans, but handles neither the triage lifecycle nor per-component VEX.
  • Regenerating an SBOM on the Dependency-Track side: we would triage something other than what was signed at build time.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
• The SBOMs in Dependency-Track are exactly those attested and signed at build time: that is the main benefit.
  • Upstream limit: Dependency-Track matches Debian advisories by source package name, while the SBOM lists binary packages (DependencyTrack/dependency-track#6132, #6957). No Debian flaw therefore shows up for golden images, and the effect of a DHI VEX on each individual flaw is not observable yet. The VEX upload itself is accepted and processed (COMPLETED).
  • dt-bridge is one more component to maintain, with its own tests (26 pytest tests).

docs.title: What would make me change my mind
docs.text: Dependency-Track importing OpenVEX natively: vex.py goes away.

docs.title: 0005 — Configure Harbor with OpenTofu rather than harbor-cli
docs.text:
In one sentence: Harbor's configuration (projects, replications, robots, retention…) is OpenTofu code with the official provider, because harbor-cli printed secrets and was not idempotent.

Status Date Scope Accepted (supersedes the initial choice of harbor-cli) September 2026 Projects, proxy caches, replications, robots, immutability, retention, webhooks, deployment security

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Harbor itself is deployed by Argo CD from its Helm chart. But its configuration lives in its database and API. It must be declarative, idempotent (a second run changes nothing) and never write a secret to Git, to logs or to plain state.

What evaluating harbor-cli (pre-1.0) found:

  • no working --password-stdin when piped: the admin password ends up in the process arguments or in an interactive prompt;
  • robot create prints the robot secret on standard output;
  • missing features: no scheduled retention, no non-interactive immutability, no namespace flattening in replication;
  • imperative commands: idempotency would have to be scripted around list/compare/create.

The Crossplane providers for Harbor are abandoned or single-maintainer, and a Crossplane control plane costs memory on a single node.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The configuration is OpenTofu code in tofu/harbor, with the official goharbor/harbor provider, run by task harbor:configure. task harbor:plan only exits 0 when nothing would change.
  • Robot secrets are generated in OpenBao and passed write-only (secret_wo, never in state).
  • The state stays local, ignored by Git, and encrypted with the OpenBao Transit key provider.
  • Replication filters name their repositories explicitly, because Harbor's github-ghcr adapter cannot list GHCR. The golden filter is derived from the catalog.

docs.title: Alternatives set aside
docs.text:
• harbor-cli: leaks secrets, not idempotent, incomplete.
  • Crossplane: unmaintained Harbor providers, memory cost.
  • curl scripts against the API: rewriting what the provider already does.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
• The dhi.io proxy cache credential and the webhook token have no write-only attribute: they are the secrets present in the encrypted state.
  • The provider does not detect every manual change (a replication filter edited in the UI does not show as drift; -replace is needed). See Lessons learned.
  • Rotating a robot secret requires bumping secret_wo_version.

docs.title: What would make me change my mind
docs.text: A harbor-cli 1.0 fixing secret handling would not be enough: the deciding argument remains being declarative.

docs.title: 0006 — Transparent registry mirror and per-namespace trust tiers
docs.text:
In one sentence: every pull goes through Harbor, but with automatic fallback to upstream, so Harbor is never a single point of failure; and admission is not imposed on the components that run it.

Status Date Scope Accepted September 2026 How nodes pull images, and what admission requires per namespace

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
We want every pull to go through Harbor (cache, scanning, a single egress point). But Harbor, its database, the CNI, the GitOps controller and the policy engine run on the same cluster. If they could only pull their images through Harbor, a Harbor outage would prevent Harbor from restarting.

Likewise, enforcing the full chain of trust on the components that implement admission would create a dependency loop.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Transparent mirror: containerd on the node has hosts.toml mirrors for docker.io, quay.io, ghcr.io, registry.k8s.io and dhi.io, pointing to the matching Harbor cache project, with upstream as fallback. Manifests keep their original references; if Harbor is down, the pull goes upstream. Bootstrap needs no special case.
  • Trust tiers by namespace label:
    • workload: full chain, enforced;
    • platform: registry allow-list and vendor signatures, in Audit mode (reported, not blocked);
    • no tier: every pod denied, so a forgotten label never turns the checks off;
    • bootstrap (kube-system, cilium, argocd, kyverno): excluded by name, see the threat model.

docs.title: Alternatives set aside
docs.text:
• Rewriting every reference to Harbor (harbor…/dockerhub-proxy/…): Harbor becomes a single point of failure for its own restart.
  • The same requirements everywhere: a dependency loop, and a cluster that can no longer converge after an outage.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
• Workloads must reference Harbor golden/apps explicitly: a docker.io reference served by the mirror is still denied, because admission sees the reference, not the actual pull path.
  • Platform components keep their upstream references and vendor signatures; their deviations are visible without blocking recovery.
  • The bootstrap exclusion is an accepted risk, limited to cluster administrators.
  • Cache fill is asynchronous and can trim multi-arch indexes (ADR 0001).

docs.title: What would make me change my mind
docs.text: A production cluster with a highly available registry outside the cluster: going through the registry could then be required for everyone.

docs.title: 0007 — Keyless signing with Sigstore, identity bound to this repository's main branch
docs.text:
In one sentence: images are signed keyless with the GitHub workflow's OIDC identity, and only this repository's main branch produces images admissible in production.

Status Date Scope Accepted, narrowed on 2026-09-28 September 2026 Signatures and attestations of golden, application and test images

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Admission must prove that an image was built by the platform's workflow, from this repository. Key-based signing assumes a private key stored, rotated and protected somewhere (a KMS or HSM in a bank); a public portfolio repository has none of that.

Sigstore keyless signing binds a short-lived Fulcio certificate to the workflow's GitHub Actions OIDC identity, and records every signature in the Rekor transparency log.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• build-image.yml signs and attests keyless with cosign v3: signature, CycloneDX SBOM, SPDX SBOM and SLSA v1 provenance.
  • Admission checks the issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com and the identity build-image.yml@refs/heads/main of this repository only.
  • Repository binding: build-image.yml is a public reusable workflow; without a check, its signing identity is the same whichever repository calls it. The build job therefore only runs if github.repository is this repository, admission requires the verified provenance to name this repository as the caller, and dt-bridge requires it in the certificate extension.
  • Signing only the digest just built: the signing steps only sign the digest this same job has just built, never a pre-existing tag on GHCR.
  • Pinned DHI key: the DHI base image signature is verified against .github/keys/dhi.pub, committed to the repository, not against a key downloaded at build time.
  • Environment-specific trust: a platform deployed from a working branch trusts that one branch in addition to main, and only in that environment (see threat model).

docs.title: Why the decision was narrowed
docs.text: The first version trusted main or any prd-* branch. Review showed that any prd-* branch could then sign images admissible in production, which is broader than intended. Since 2026-09-28: main only by default, plus repository binding, signing only the digest just built, and the pinned DHI key.

docs.title: Alternatives set aside
docs.text:
• A classic cosign key in a GitHub secret: a long-lived key to protect and rotate, for no gain here.
  • A key in a KMS: the right answer in a bank, but there is no KMS in a portfolio. Switching only changes the attestor definition in the policies.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
• No private key to manage; every signature is public and auditable in Rekor.
  • Signing and verification depend on the public Sigstore infrastructure (Fulcio, Rekor, TUF root).
  • Write access to main is part of the chain of trust. The ruleset blocks deletion and force-pushes, not who can push. Here, that is the sole owner.
  • After each working branch merge, pinned images must be re-pinned (release-repin.yml).

docs.title: What would make me change my mind
docs.text: A regulated context: a KMS/HSM key or a private Sigstore, required reviews and restricted pushes to main.

docs.title: 0008 — Grype and Trivy diverge: Dependency-Track is authoritative
docs.text:
In one sentence: three scanners look at the same images and give different CVE lists; we do not reconcile them and never add them up, we triage in Dependency-Track.

Status Date Scope Accepted September 2026 Which vulnerability counts are authoritative

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Three scanners look at the same images:

  • Trivy in CI (build-image.yml), enforcing, with the base image's VEX;
  • Trivy in Harbor (scan on push, deployment security);
  • Grype in the cluster (Kubescape), on running images.

Trivy and Grype share neither vulnerability databases, nor matching algorithms, nor the way they apply VEX. Their lists diverge, sometimes on severity, sometimes on whether a CVE is present at all. Dependency-Track matches the attested SBOM against its own sources.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Trivy remains the build gate (CI) and the registry gate (Harbor).
  • Grype remains Kubescape's own view of running images; it is not reconciled with Trivy.
  • Dependency-Track, fed by dt-bridge, is the triage source of truth. The image posture dashboard labels each CVE count with its source (harbor-trivy, dependency-track), before and after VEX.

docs.title: Alternatives set aside
docs.text:
• A single scanner everywhere: Kubescape embeds Grype, and Trivy is Harbor's native scanner; replacing either would lose an integration.
  • Adding up or merging counts: we would count the same flaw twice, or hide a useful disagreement.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
• A CVE can block a build in Trivy and be absent from Grype, or the reverse. Each tool is read on its own terms, and triage happens in Dependency-Track.
  • The dashboard never adds up the counts of two scanners.
